To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the differentiation of neuroblastoma cells into osteogenic lineage can be obtained by rapamycin treatment; 2) the differentiation of the same neuroblastoma cells in hepatic lineage can be obtained without an intermediate 'pluripotent stem cell' step.
the mTOR inhibitor rapamycin is able to differentiate neuroblastoma cells into osteoblastic and hepatic lineage.

1) the inhibition of the mTOR pathway induces the differentiation of human neuroblastomas cells into osteoblasts, and 2) the inhibition of mTOR pathway induces also the differentiation of human cancer cells into hepatocytes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the possibility to control cell fate by manipulating the metabolic activity, and it opens a new way for a more efficient therapy of tumors.
a better comprehension of the mechanisms underlying the cell fate decision.
the possibility to manipulate cancer cells toward a normal phenotype by using a pharmacological approach.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the cell fate is controlled by the interaction of a few molecules and the scaffold, in the presence of an altered metabolism.
cancer cells are plastic and can change their fate by a process of 'dedifferentiation' and/or 'trans-differentiation', depending on the environmental cues and the genetic background.
the 'in vitro' differentiation of cancer cells is a process of reprogramming of gene and protein expression, which is not necessarily dependent on a stem cell intermediate step.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

1) neuroblastoma cells are not able to differentiate directly in the mesoderm lineage (as osteoblasts); 2) rapamycin is not sufficient to differentiate neuroblastoma cells in osteoblasts; 3) the presence of a specific scaffold is necessary for the differentiation of neuroblastoma cells into osteoblasts and hepatic lineage.
a cancer cell is not a terminally differentiated cell, but a cell that can be reprogrammed toward different cell lineages.

the differentiation is not a 'one-step' process and that the cell fate is not only determined by the expression of few genes, but also by the presence of the correct microenvironment and metabolic changes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
cancer cells can be differentiated toward a non-tumor cell type, by modulating their metabolism.
the differentiation process can be controlled and directed in the laboratory, opening the possibility of developing new therapies for cancer patients.
the metabolic reprogramming is the key event that controls the cell fate and differentiation.
